 Read the passage below and then answer questions 26 to 38
 Murimi drove slowly down the Government road eager to attend the celebration. Everyone in the car
 was quite, thinking about the people who had sacrificed their lives so that Harry Thuku, the freedom
 fighter could be set free. Little Naiku was fascinated by Nyanjiru, the woman who had led men, woman
 and children in fighting for freedom, so long ago.
 “Papa,” she called her father, “when we gain independence tonight and the white men are gone, who
 shall lead us then?”
 “Ah, a good question, my child, “Murimi replied, “we shall have our own government. A government
 of Kenyans and Kenyans. We shall elect out own leaders.”
 Naiku asked again, “Will ‘mamas’ lead us too?”
 “No!” Njoroge shouted. “This will be a government of black men. Our government.”
 “Why men?” Naiku cried agrily.
 “When did you ever hear of a black ‘mama’ leading men?” Njoroge asked.
 “Mama Nyanjiru was a leader of men,” Naikyu protested.
 “You are right, Naiku,” said grandpa.
 “Even in the forest where we fought the white man, woman fought just as bravely. General Muthoni was
 one of the bravest warriors I even met – braver than most men I know. Only a fool or a coward says that a
 woman cannot lead. Of course, they can and will lead.”
 At that moment, a car with a white driver overtook them and Njoroge shouted, “Settlers, settlers go
 home!” Murimi was furous.
 “Njoroge!” he said, how dare you misbehaved like that? You will have to answer for it when we
 get home!”
 “Does independence day make you lose your manners? That man is a grown up, older that even
 your father, “added grandpa.
 “We did not fight the white men our independence so that our children can behave like them. You
 were never brought up to abuse people,” Murimi said angrily. Njoroge was quiet for a long time. He
 thought long and hard about his grandpa’s words. He was sorry for the way he had acted.
 (Adapted from A big struggle by A. Amran and D. Mulwa. Oxford University Press)

 Read the passage below and answer questions 39 to 50
 Many people all over the world still smoke although it is common knowledge that smoking is
 dangerous to health. This was nicotine found in the cigarettes has been proven to be addictive. Many
 young people get introduced to this habit through peer pressure, by aping their parents of the celebrities
 they watched on TV advertisements.
 Today, smokers give various reasons for maintaining this habit. They say cigarettes are useful
 stimulates and that thy give the smokers something to do with their hands. Perhaps the most important
 cause for the increase in smoking is provides shared experience among the peer group and this continues
 even after it becomes a settled habit at what point it actually becomes a habit difficult to shake off, is not
 possible to tell.
 The aggressive campaign through advertisement and advocacy by manufactures has made things worse.
 Manufactures argue that smoking provides employment through tobacco farming, manufacturing
 industries and contributes directly to the economy through payment taxes. However, the government
 spends three times as much for the treatment of smoking related ailments and on rehabilitation of smokers.
 The arguments against smoking are very valid. It can at times by very expensive for smokers and has
 no social advantage. The smoke from smokers is harmful and offensive to those around them (secondary
 smokers). It also interferes with teamwork since those who smoke keep excusing themselves to go and
 smoke. We know that tobacco stains the hands of smokers and makes the smokers have bad breath. In
 addition, it shortens one’s breath, making it difficult for one to participate in the activities which demand a
 lot of energy, such as atheletics. But these are minor objectives when we consider damage it can do to
 one’s health. There is enough evidence that smoking causes bronchitis and hearts disease, both of which
 can be fatal. It is therefore advisable for the young people to distance, both from this habit it they want to
 live a health life.
